title: Along Came Polly
full_review:
By looking at the poster of the Ben Stiller-Jennifer Aniston coupling, "Along Came Polly" (Universal), one would expect a breezy romantic comedy full of love, laughs and a ferret. Well, at least director John Hamburg delivers on the ferret. And though one out of three is not bad, the movie is.

In lieu of a smart, witty farce about the emotional perils of modern mating, Hamburg dwells mainly in the loo, stringing together a series of crude bathroom and boudoir sight gags made more painful by his love-shy leads' total lack of on-screen chemistry.

Stiller stars as Reuben Feffer, an ace risk assessor for a leading New York insurance firm who has the rug pulled out from under his hypercalculated life when he catches his wife, Lisa (Debra Messing), in a compromising position with a buff (and in-the-buff) scuba instructor (Hank Azaria) on the first day of their dream Caribbean honeymoon. Jilted before the ink has even dried on their marriage license, he returns home alone, where he is coaxed back into the social saddle by his best friend, Sandy (Philip Seymour Hoffman), a former teen celebrity trying to jump-start his washed-up career by hiring a TV crew to document his comeback performance in a community theater production of "Jesus Christ Superstar." While licking his wounds at a party in a trendy SoHo art gallery, Reuben runs into Polly (Aniston), a bohemian free spirit from his junior high school days.

At first it seems like no two people could be less likely to hit it off. Impulsive and noncommittal, Polly's rolling-stone-gathers-no-moss spontaneity flies in the face of Reuben's obsessive play-it-safe, nothing-ventured-nothing-lost philosophy of life. Also, her penchant for exotic, spicy food wreaks havoc with his irritable bowel syndrome.

Using their utter incompatibility as a launching pad, the dopey narrative nosedives into a bog of scatological skits involving clogged toilets and Polly's visually impaired pet ferret, with dollops of assorted bodily fluids and tasteless stock sexual jokes thrown in for bad measure. And though the road to overcoming their differences hits a speed bump in the person of Lisa, who returns repentant and looking for a second shot at marital bliss, Reuben and Polly's preordained pairing is never in doubt.

Rounding out the cast are Bryan Brown as Leyland Van Lew, an Australian daredevil Reuben is hired to assess, and Alec Baldwin as Stan Indursky, Reuben's flatulent, borscht-belt boss who provides most of the film's guilty chuckles.

A romantic comedy's success is determined by the audience's desire to see its leads together by the closing credits. In the case of "Along Came Polly," thanks to a monumental mismatch in casting, viewers' rooting interest remains cool at best.

Aniston seems lost on the big screen, her sitcom effervescence much better suited for TV, while the talents of Stiller -- who seems to be carving a career for himself as a hip, borderline-postal, yuppie neurotic -- are wasted on what is essentially a one-joke role. Throughout the film, Stiller's character spouts off the risk percentages of being struck by lightning or falling into a subway grating; perhaps the more pertinent data would be the career risks involved with choosing bad scripts.

Buried somewhere beneath the potty humor and stale scenarios is a message about taking risks and the serendipity of love, but it's not worth the dig. While the film may prove opposites attract, it may prove harder attracting moviegoers.

Due to a few sexual encounters, much crass humor, some rear nudity, recurring crude language and profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
